description: One-person team from Medellín, Colombia, participating virtually. I build software and AI tools that turn complex NASA and geospatial data into something anyone can explore and understand. Background in 3D modeling and coordinate systems, now focused on web apps and AI agents. Not recruiting — this is a solo mission.
summary: Mars Walk Planner is an interactive 3D map that helps the first astronauts on Mars plan a safe walk on Mount Sharp, Gale crater, where Curiosity is driving today. On a 1 m HiRISE terrain model it computes least-cost walking routes from a hypothetical habitat to seven destinations Curiosity actually studied, avoiding slopes steeper than 15°. For each route it shows the elevation profile, walking time at Apollo-based paces, the return margin and an estimated radiation dose. A "Mars today" tab adds Curiosity's latest REMS weather, DONKI space weather and rover photos. Every number is checked: Curiosity's published track was aligned to the terrain (1.66 m spread at 467 control stops) and all 28 routes were verified metre by metre. Where no safe route exists, the map says so. All the terrain is real NASA data: the HiRISE elevation model and photo at 1 m per pixel. Nothing is invented.
details:
What it does

Mars Walk Planner is the planning screen a crew could use from a habitat on Mount Sharp, Gale crater, before going out on foot. It works on a 3.5 km × 3.5 km area of Curiosity's real path, shown in 3D from a 1 m HiRISE terrain model (relief exaggerated 3×, stated on screen).

  • Ten fixed points: a hypothetical habitat, seven destinations that Curiosity actually studied (with what the science team found there and a link to the mission blog), and two isolated sites that no safe walk can reach.
  • Routes: pick a destination and the map draws the least-cost safe route, an animated walker, the elevation and slope profile, the walking time, the time left at the destination and the return margin for the chosen outing length.
  • Astronaut paces: three paces with a source (3.6, 2.7 and 1.7 km/h on flat ground, from Apollo records); speed changes with slope following Tobler's hiking function.
  • Radiation: estimated dose for the outing from the average measured by RAD on Curiosity (Hassler et al. 2013).
  • Mars today: Curiosity's latest REMS weather, the latest coronal mass ejection reaching Mars from DONKI (WSA-ENLIL), and Navcam and Mastcam photos taken at each destination.
  • Layers: real HiRISE photo (grey, as the camera sees it), an approximate "Martian tint" labelled as such, colour by elevation, and Curiosity's track aligned to the terrain.
  • Entrance globe (Viking mosaic) that flies to Gale crater, a 30-step guided tour, Spanish and English, and light and dark themes.

How it works

A Python pipeline reads the HiRISE terrain model, computes slope and runs A* in two stages: first on a 5 m grid, then a 1 m search inside a 100 m corridor around that route, with a small safety margin. Slopes above 15° are obstacles (limit taken from the MoonPath lunar traverse study, Peña-Asensio et al. 2024), and destinations sit within 2 km of the habitat, as in that study. All routes are precomputed and published as a single static web page built with Three.js, so it works without a server.

How we checked it

  • Curiosity's published positions were 55–97 m off the terrain model (within its stated accuracy). We measured and corrected the offset per segment; at 467 control stops not used for the fit, the terrain elevation matches the rover's with a 1.66 m spread.
  • All 28 routes were verified metre by metre on the 1 m terrain: none steps on a cell steeper than 15°. Another 17 pairs of points have no safe route, and the map says so.
  • Our terrain reader matches Global Mapper v20 (independent GIS software) with a largest error of 0.73 mm at 238 points; we also compared elevation and slope profiles and Curiosity's track there.
  • Terrain slope against the tilt Curiosity measured at 933 stops: 9.3° against 9.6° on average; stop by stop the relation is moderate (r = 0.55), below the 0.6 goal we set. We report it as it is.
  • The HiRISE photo matches the terrain within 1–3 m.

Limits (shown in the app)

There is no rock map: obstacles are avoided by slope only. Walking speeds come from the Moon, not Mars; Tobler's function was measured on Earth; the dose does not include solar storms; space weather is a simulation; REMS data arrive months late; the habitat is hypothetical, not a NASA-selected site.

Why it matters

The first Marswalks will be limited by slope, distance and time. This tool turns NASA orbital and rover data into a clear go / no-go answer for each walk, with the numbers behind it and an honest list of what is not validated.

Tools

Python (numpy, pandas, Pillow), JavaScript, Three.js, and Global Mapper v20 for validation. Source code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/CauseofDeathLife/mars-walk-planner

Use of AI

The idea, the choice of challenge, the design of the tool and the validation plan are the author's, and the author ran the manual checks in Global Mapper. Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding and research assistant: it wrote most of the code under the author's direction and helped check data and draft these texts, the README and the demo slides. Claude Code was used during preparation. The team emblem was generated with Gemini (Google) and carries a visible "AI-generated image" watermark; Gemini was also used to summarize the official submission video. No NASA logos or mission identifiers were generated or modified with AI.
